verses.text: Listen to this word which I take up for a lamentation over you, O house of Israel.
“The virgin of Israel has fallen; She shall rise no more. She is cast down on her land; there is no one to raise her up.”
For thus says the Lord Yahweh: “The city that went out a thousand shall have a hundred left, and that which went out one hundred shall have ten left to the house of Israel.”
For Yahweh says to the house of Israel: “Seek me, and you will live;
but don’t seek Bethel, nor enter into Gilgal, and don’t pass to Beersheba: for Gilgal shall surely go into captivity, and Bethel shall come to nothing.
Seek Yahweh, and you will live; lest he break out like fire in the house of Joseph, and it devour, and there be no one to quench it in Bethel.
You who turn justice to wormwood, and cast down righteousness to the earth:

seek him who made the Pleiades and Orion, and turns the shadow of death into the morning, and makes the day dark with night; who calls for the waters of the sea, and pours them out on the surface of the earth, Yahweh is his name,
who brings sudden destruction on the strong, so that destruction comes on the fortress.
They hate him who reproves in the gate, and they abhor him who speaks blamelessly.

Therefore, because you trample on the poor, and take taxes from him of wheat: You have built houses of cut stone, but you will not dwell in them. You have planted pleasant vineyards, but you shall not drink their wine.
For I know how many your offenses, and how great are your sins — you who afflict the just, who take a bribe, and who turn aside the needy in the courts.
Therefore a prudent person keeps silent in such a time, for it is an evil time.
Seek good, and not evil, that you may live; and so Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be with you, as you say.
Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts. It may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.”

Therefore Yahweh, the God of Armies, the Lord, says: “Wailing will be in all the wide ways; and they will say in all the streets, ‘Alas! Alas!’ and they will call the farmer to mourning, and those who are skillful in lamentation to wailing.
In all vineyards there will be wailing; for I will pass through the middle of you,” says Yahweh.
“Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! Why do you long for the day of Yahweh? It is darkness, and not light.
As if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him; Or he went into the house and leaned his hand on the wall, and a snake bit him.
Won’t the day of Yahweh be darkness, and not light? Even very dark, and no brightness in it?
I hate, I despise your feasts, and I can’t stand your solemn assemblies.
Yes, though you offer me your burnt offerings and meal offerings, I will not accept them; neither will I regard the peace offerings of your fat animals.
Take away from me the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps.
But let justice roll on like rivers, and righteousness like a mighty stream.
“Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel?
You also carried the tent of your king and the shrine of your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves.
Therefore will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus,” says Yahweh, whose name is the God of Armies.

footnotes.content: Amos doesn't begin with polite words—he takes up a lamentation, a funeral dirge, for Israel while she still lives. He speaks as one who grieves what is about to be lost. This is what a faithful prophet does: he names the death that disobedience is bringing, hoping the people might yet hear and turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The virgin of Israel—a tender image for a maiden in her beauty—has fallen never to rise again. When we reject the one who made us, we forfeit not just our dignity but the very strength we thought was ours. Yet even here, in a word framed as final, there is room for the mercy of the Lord to surprise us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A thousand soldiers reduced to a hundred, a hundred to ten—such are the hidden costs of turning away from God. The Lord speaks in measured numbers, showing that every loss traces back to a choice. Justice is not arbitrary; it follows faithfully upon what we have sown.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Here is the pivot: Seek me, and you will live. Even as the prophet names judgment, the Lord extends his hand. The same God who warns is also the one who says 'if you turn to me, life returns.' In every word of judgment there hides an invitation to mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't seek Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba—the very shrines where they thought to find blessing. False gods in holy places are most dangerous because they feel familiar. The Lord is saying: stop searching for me in the temples of your own making, for those sanctuaries will lead you into captivity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seek Yahweh, and you will live. The same command as verse 4, but now Amos adds urgency: 'lest he break out like fire.' The Lord's justice is not far off; it presses near. He repeats the invitation because he means it, and time is short for those who still have ears to hear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To turn justice to wormwood and cast righteousness down to the earth—this is the sin at the root of all the others. When a people abandon the pursuit of what is right and fair, everything that follows is corruption. Amos names the thing God hates: not ignorance, but the deliberate twisting of goodness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seek him who made the Pleiades and Orion—Amos suddenly lifts our gaze to the heavens. The Lord who commands the stars is the same one who summons shadow into morning and calls the waters of the sea. To seek him is to seek One whose power is woven through all creation, whose faithfulness never falters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He brings sudden destruction on the strong—the mighty find no refuge when they stand against the Lord. This is comfort to the weak and warning to the proud. No fortress, no strength of arm, can hold back his judgment. Only surrender and repentance offer shelter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They hate him who reproves in the gate—the city gate where disputes were settled and justice should have been done. Instead of welcoming correction, the people have turned against truth-tellers. This is how a nation dies: when it punishes the honest and rewards the comfortable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You have built houses of cut stone, but you will not dwell in them—the bitter irony of ill-gotten gain. The houses they built through injustice to the poor will become their tombs, not their homes. The Lord takes away what was never righteously theirs to begin with.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: For I know how many your offenses—the Lord knows the exact weight of their sin. He counts every injustice, every bribe taken, every poor person turned away. This is not careless judgment; it is the reckoning of One who has seen everything and forgets nothing. Yet even knowing all this, he offers verse 4 again.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A prudent person keeps silent in such a time—when evil has taken root so deeply that speaking truth only brings danger, even the wise may find themselves holding their tongue. It's a hard word for hard times, a recognition that sometimes darkness advances faster than light can speak.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seek good, and not evil, that you may live—a clear choice placed before them. The path is simple enough to understand: choose what is good, reject what is evil, and life will follow. The God of Armies will be with those who make this choice. The door stands open.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hate evil, love good, and establish justice in the courts—Amos makes the call concrete. It's not enough to merely dislike wickedness; we must actively hate it and pursue its opposite. And we must do this where it matters most: in the places where justice is meant to be done, where the weak stand before the powerful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wailing will be in all the wide ways—the public squares, the places where life happens, will be filled with mourning. The Lord paints a picture of a nation utterly broken. Even the farmer, who knows the land's rhythms, will be called to mourning. No one will be spared the grief that comes from exile.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In all vineyards there will be wailing—the fields they planted hoping for harvest will become places of lament. The Lord himself will pass through their land in judgment. What they planted with their own hands becomes the place of their undoing. Yet even this—'I will pass through'—leaves room for one who might see him and live.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Woe to you who desire the day of Yahweh! They long for his judgment thinking it will vindicate them, not realizing it will expose them. How often do we imagine the Lord's hand will fall on our enemies but pass over us? Amos warns: be careful what you ask for, for his light reveals all.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him—no escape, no refuge. He runs into a house only to find a snake. This is the desperation of the day of judgment: everywhere you turn, danger meets you. The Lord is illustrating that there is no hiding place when his judgment comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Won't the day of Yahweh be darkness, and not light? The repetition hammers home the truth: they expect vindication but will find only darkness. It is a day even darker than night, empty of all consolation for those who have turned from him. The only light in that day will shine on the righteous remnant.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I hate, I despise your feasts, and I can't stand your solemn assemblies—the Lord turns his face from their worship. They still offer the rituals, still gather in his name, but without justice in their hearts, their songs are only noise. He makes plain what breaks his heart: worship divorced from righteousness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Though you offer me your burnt offerings and meal offerings, I will not accept them—no sacrifice can substitute for a changed heart. The fattest offerings of their best animals mean nothing to the Lord when they come from hands stained with injustice. He turns away, not from cruelty, but because their worship is empty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Take away from me the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps—their music has become a distraction from the cry of the oppressed. Beautiful melodies mean nothing to a God who hears the silence of those who have no voice. He silences the harp so he can listen to what truly matters.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: But let justice roll on like rivers, and righteousness like a mighty stream—here is what the Lord actually wants. Not ceremony or song, but justice flowing in abundance, righteousness running like water that cannot be stopped. This is the worship he receives gladly: a people committed to doing what is right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel?—the Lord reminds them of the covenant relationship forged in the desert. For forty years, before they built temples or established formal worship, they walked with him. Now they have the buildings but have forgotten the God who led them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: You also carried the tent of your king and the shrine of your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves—even in the wilderness, they were divided. Half their heart was with the Lord, half with the idols they had fashioned. No wonder they are broken: a house divided cannot stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Therefore will I cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus—the Lord names exile as the end, yet readers today hear an echo in this word: even captivity is not the final word of the God who loves his people. Beyond exile, in the mercy that always outlasts judgment, the Lord restores the tent of David. His faithfulness endures beyond Damascus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
